conceptTag: What automation means for a translation agency
readerTitle: When the first draft costs nothing: a translation agency's next move
caseNote: 가상 사례 (번역 에이전시, 호텔 그룹 고객, 앱 회사) · 수치 없음. 기계 번역 초안과 사람 검수를 섞는 방식은 업계에서 널리 쓰이는 일반적인 관행으로만 서술
insight: 자동화가 들어오면 '무엇이 싸졌나'보다 '무엇이 여전히 귀한가'를 먼저 묻고, 그 귀한 부분을 따로 팔아야 가치를 지킬 수 있다.
misconception: 기계가 초안을 공짜로 만들어 주면 그 절감분은 그대로 우리 이익이 된다. 또는 품질을 내세워 전부 사람이 하면 가격을 지킬 수 있다.

sources.text: 설명용 가상 사례. 특정 기업이나 통계를 인용하지 않음
기계 번역 + 사람 사후 편집(post-editing)은 번역 업계의 일반적인 작업 방식

factChecks.note: 모든 인물, 회사, 상황은 가상입니다. 카드에 구체적인 단가, 비율, 품질 수치를 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 수치가 추가되지 않았는지 확인하세요.
'기계 번역 품질은 언어 쌍과 문서 종류에 따라 다르다', '초안 생성 비용이 거의 0에 가까워졌다'는 일반적 서술입니다. 과장으로 읽히지 않는지 검토하세요.
알레르기 정보와 환불·취소 규정을 '사람이 확인할 고위험 문구'로 든 것은 설명용 판단입니다. 특정 국가의 표시 의무나 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않게 표현했는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: When the first draft costs nothing
body: Mina runs a 12-person translation agency. For years, her team sold one thing: words, priced per word.
Now a machine drafts a hotel's entire website in seconds. Her translators can do it. Her rivals can do it. And her clients have noticed they can do it too.

image.label: A translator's desk with a machine draft appearing instantly on screen
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 사무실 책상, 모니터에 여러 언어의 문서가 한순간에 채워지는 모션 라인. 옆에 빨간 펜과 종이 교정본을 든 번역가가 생각에 잠긴 표정. 실제 소프트웨어나 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your biggest client wants half price.
body: A hotel group sends Mina a message: "Machine translation is basically free now. Cut your rate in half, or we'll do it in-house."
Their work covers room descriptions, FAQs, restaurant menus, booking terms and a new brand campaign. What should Mina do?

options.text: Cut the rate in half on everything to keep the client
options.feedback: She keeps the account, but every saving from the tool flows to the client. That's **who captures value** at work: when everyone has the same tool, the customer usually wins the savings.

options.text: Refuse and promise that humans will translate every word
options.feedback: It protects quality where it matters, but she'd charge full price for routine text the client can now get elsewhere. She may lose the whole account over the cheap parts.

options.text: Split the work: machine drafts plus a quick check for routine text, full human work for menus, terms and the campaign
options.feedback: This is **what to automate and what to keep human**. She lowers the price where errors are cheap and protects it where mistakes hurt.

cards.title: The tool made drafts cheap for everyone.
body: Mina's costs fell. But so did everyone else's, and the client's own costs fell too.
When a tool is available to all sides, savings rarely stay with the seller. Competition passes them to customers. That's why per-word prices for routine text keep sliding.
So the real question isn't how much cheaper Mina can work. It's **what she still has that the tool doesn't** give away for free.

cards.title: Not every word carries the same risk.
body: Mina sorts the hotel's work by one test: what happens if a sentence is wrong?

breakdown.label: Room amenities, FAQs
breakdown.detail: Errors are cheap and easy to spot. Machine draft, quick human check.

breakdown.label: Menus with allergen notes
breakdown.detail: A small error can make a guest sick. A person reviews every line.

breakdown.label: Booking and cancellation terms
breakdown.detail: A wrong word can cost money or start a dispute.

breakdown.label: Brand campaign
breakdown.detail: Tone and culture matter. A person writes, not just fixes.

cards.title: Automate where mistakes are cheap.
body: From **What to automate and what to keep human**: hand work to machines when errors are cheap, easy to notice and easy to fix. Keep people where errors are costly, hard to see, or need judgment about people.
A clumsy line about towels annoys nobody. A mistranslated allergy warning can hurt a guest, and the hotel might not notice until it does.

image.label: Two-by-two grid: cost of error vs how easy it is to spot
image.brief: 2x2 매트릭스 인포그래픽. 가로축 "How easy to spot the error", 세로축 "Cost of an error". 왼쪽 아래 "Room amenities"(Automate), 오른쪽 위 "Allergen notes", "Cancellation terms"(Keep human). 따뜻한 파스텔 톤, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Sell the scarce part, not the words.
body: Using **Who captures value**: Mina can only charge for what clients can't easily get elsewhere.
Drafts are no longer scarce. Her team's knowledge of the hotel's brand terms, careful review of risky text, and willingness to sign off on the result still are.
So she changes what she sells. Instead of one per-word rate, she offers a low price for checked machine drafts and a separate fee for reviewed, launch-ready content she stands behind.

cards.title: The line between them keeps moving.
body: Machine quality improves, and it varies by language pair and type of text. What needs a person today may not need one next year. Mina has to re-sort the work regularly, not once.
There's a second risk. Clients rarely see the value of a check until something goes wrong. If she can't show what her review catches, they'll treat it as a cost to cut.

cards.title: Now it's an app going global.
body: You run a budgeting app. You want to launch in 12 languages next quarter. Your users will see buttons, help articles, the checkout screen, subscription terms and your app store page.

options.feedback: Fast and cheap, but a confusing checkout or wrong subscription term costs sales and trust. Those errors are costly and hard for you to spot in a language you don't read.

options.text: Hire human translators for all 12 languages
options.feedback: Safe, but slow and expensive for buttons and help pages where small errors are cheap. You'd pay human rates for work a machine plus users' feedback can handle.

options.text: Machine for buttons and help articles, with an in-app "report a translation" link; human review for checkout, terms and store pages
options.feedback: **What to automate and what to keep human** again: automate where errors are cheap and easy to catch, pay for people where a mistake costs money or trust.

cards.title: When a tool makes work cheap, sell what's still scarce.
body: Concepts used: **What to automate and what to keep human** sorted the work by the cost of an error. **Who captures value** showed why savings drift to customers, and why Mina must price the scarce part separately.
**Try it today:** list five tasks your business sells. Mark each one: cheap to get wrong, or costly to get wrong. Are you pricing them the same way?
